query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3, exposure to high-temperature oxidizing environments promotes preferential segregation of Ti and Al to grain boundaries to form continuous, non-protective oxide layers that weaken intergranular cohesion and promote catastrophic failure, while reducing environments suppress this segregation and delay degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: An additively manufactured HEA with a homogeneous FCC matrix, minimal pre‐existing oxides, and a refined microstructure typical of AM processes.
generation.intervention: Expose samples to a controlled elevated temperature (around 850°C) in either an oxidizing atmosphere (e.g., air or high oxygen partial pressure gas) or a reducing atmosphere (e.g., hydrogen-rich gas).
generation.conditions: Testing at temperatures between 800–900°C for exposure durations up to 100 hours under gas atmospheres with well‐controlled oxygen levels; comparisons made between oxidizing conditions (oxygen partial pressure ≥0.21 atm) and reducing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundaries that become enriched with Ti- and Al-rich oxide layers due to preferential diffusion and oxidation at high temperatures.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, Ti and Al atoms diffuse to grain boundaries where they oxidize forming a continuous yet non-protective oxide scale. This oxide layer limits cohesive strength across grain boundaries and acts as a site for crack initiation. In contrast, reducing environments limit oxide formation, thus preserving intergranular cohesion and delaying failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under oxidizing conditions, the oxide layer at grain boundaries will thicken, leading to an increased density of intergranular cracks and a significant reduction in tensile and creep strength relative to the as-manufactured state. Under reducing conditions, oxide formation will be suppressed, maintaining a microstructure similar to the baseline with superior mechanical performance.
generation.baseline: The as-manufactured alloy exhibits a uniform FCC microstructure with low levels of intergranular oxides and intact grain boundaries, resulting in optimal high-temperature mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: This behavior is expected within the tested temperature range of 800–900°C and under gas environments with oxygen partial pressures typical of air (or higher for oxidizing tests) versus hydrogen-rich conditions for reducing tests; deviations may occur outside these specific thermal and atmospheric conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The exact kinetics of Ti and Al segregation and the consequent oxide growth rate as well as the potential influence of residual AM-induced defects on oxidation behavior require further quantitative investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a set of additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 samples and subject them to 850°C for 100 hours under two controlled gas atmospheres: one oxidizing (air or oxygen-enriched) and one reducing (hydrogen-rich). After exposure, conduct detailed microstructural characterization (via SEM/EDS and XRD) to assess the presence, thickness, and continuity of oxide layers along grain boundaries, and perform mechanical tests (tensile and creep) to quantify any loss in strength.
measurements: Grain boundary oxide thickness and composition via SEM/EDS
Crack density and distribution via optical microscopy
Tensile yield strength and creep life measurements
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples exposed in an oxidizing atmosphere do not exhibit significantly thicker, continuous Ti-/Al-rich oxide layers at grain boundaries along with a measurable reduction in mechanical properties compared to both the reducing environment and the as-manufactured baseline, then the hypothesis that oxide-induced intergranular weakening governs degradation and catastrophic failure is falsified.

System: CoCrFeNiTi high-entropy alloy (equimolar or nearly equimolar proportions of Cobalt, Chromium, Iron, Nickel, and Titanium). Processing: Mechanical alloying using a planetary ball mill (QM-1SP4) at 400 rpm for 1–6 hours under argon atmosphere, followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) in a vacuum at 900–1000 °C for 10 minutes with a heating rate of 50 °C/min.
